primitives.name: Era Normalization Factor
primitives.verbatim_quote: Method / model - Era normalization: nf = ⟨Team runs⟩_all / ⟨Team runs⟩_year multiplies runs scored/conceded (borrowed from citation normalization, Radicchi et al.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'nf': 'dimensionless normalization factor', '\\langle \\text{Team runs} \\rangle_{\\text{all}}': 'mean team runs across all eras', '\\langle \\text{Team runs} \\rangle_{\\text{year}}': 'mean team runs in specific year'}
primitives.assumptions: Performance metrics are multiplicatively separable from era-specific scaling; team run rates are representative of era context.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When team run rates are not indicative of era context or data spans are insufficient.

layer2.mapping: Used in GSI to adjust raw performance values for temporal variance; in GSE, applied to normalize match-level stats for inter-era comparability.
layer2.telemetry: Normalized performance deviation from expected era baseline.

primitives.name: Fractional Contribution
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Fractional contribution: fc = 1⁄2·(runs scored/total team runs + wickets taken/total team wickets) ∈ [0,1]; specialists capped at 0.5.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'fc': 'dimensionless fractional contribution', '\\text{runs scored}': 'individual runs scored', '\\text{team runs}': 'total team runs', '\\text{wickets taken}': 'individual wickets taken', '\\text{team wickets}': 'total team wickets'}
primitives.assumptions: Runs and wickets are valid performance proxies; contribution shares sum to 1 across a team.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When team performance is dominated by outliers or when contribution is not evenly distributed.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSI’s probabilistic scoring of player impact; in GSE, used to assess player centrality in team dynamics.
layer2.telemetry: Player's share of team performance in normalized units.

primitives.name: Effective Team Size
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Effective team size: S_eff = 2^H, H = -Σ_c fc log2 fc (entropy of contribution distribution).
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'S_{\\text{eff}}': 'dimensionless effective team size', 'H': 'entropy of contribution distribution', 'f_c': 'fractional contribution of player c'}
primitives.assumptions: Contribution distribution is stationary; entropy reflects team balance and vulnerability.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When team composition is highly skewed or when entropy cannot be reliably estimated.

layer2.mapping: In GSI, used as an injury-vulnerability index; in GSE, models team resilience and adaptability under player loss.
layer2.telemetry: Entropy-derived measure of team dispersion and stability.

primitives.name: Shuffle-Null Hot-Streak Test
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Null models: shuffle performance timestamps (100×) per player for individual hot streaks; shuffle match-result timestamps (104×) holding win count for team streaks.
primitives.assumptions: Streaks are not due to inherent skill unless statistically significant compared to shuffled data.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When data is insufficient or when temporal dependencies are not captured by shuffling.

layer2.mapping: In GSI, used to validate streak significance; in GSE, to detect false positive performance clustering.
layer2.telemetry: Statistical significance of observed streaks against null-hypothesis distributions.

The four primitives form a coherent framework for analyzing cricket performance through scalable, normalized, and probabilistically grounded lenses. The era normalization factor adjusts for temporal variance in run rates, enabling fair comparison across decades. Fractional contribution quantifies individual impact within team contexts, with a cap for specialists ensuring bounded influence. Effective team size, derived from entropy, captures team balance and vulnerability—key for injury-risk modeling. Shuffle-null tests provide statistical rigor to detect genuine streaks, avoiding spurious correlations. These operators are mathematically dual in structure: normalization and contribution are additive, while entropy and null testing are complementary. Failure modes include overfitting in small datasets, misapplication of normalization where context varies, and entropy collapse in highly centralized teams. The framework supports both individual and collective analysis, aligning with GSI's Bayesian inference and GSE's state-transition logic.
